messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 72
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Refugee Aid Worker
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 53

Mr. Nguyen, at 72, carries a quiet dignity, his face etched with a lifetime of compassion and hardship. His eyes, though often weary now, still hold a spark of the dedication that has defined his career as a refugee aid worker. Six months ago, that dedication was tested in a way he never anticipated, even after decades spent in conflict zones. He sits across from me, his hands clasped, recounting the day the world shifted.

It was a Tuesday, a day like any other, in a bustling market square he knew intimately. He was there, not for aid distribution, but to simply enjoy a cup of jasmine tea, observing the vibrant life he had helped rebuild in a community ravaged by war. He remembers the warmth of the sun, the chatter of vendors, the smell of freshly baked bread. Then, the world exploded. A deafening roar, a shockwave that threw him to the ground, followed by a rain of debris, dust, and screams. He recalls the immediate disorientation, the ringing in his ears, and the metallic taste of fear. His first instinct, honed by years of crisis, was to help. He pushed himself up, his body aching, and navigated through the chaos. He saw unspeakable things: the injured, the lifeless, the terror in the eyes of survivors. He tried to pull people from the rubble, his hands frantic, but the scale of devastation was overwhelming. He remembers holding a young child, barely older than his own grandson, whose eyes stared blankly upwards. He survived, physically bruised but internally shattered, while so many around him did not.

In the weeks that followed, Mr. Nguyen found himself caught in a new kind of war, an internal one. The physical wounds healed, but the invisible ones deepened. Sleep became a battleground, haunted by vivid nightmares of the explosion. He would wake in a cold sweat, the scent of burning plastic and the screams of the injured still fresh in his mind, feeling as if he was back in the dust and chaos of the market. During the day, sudden noises – a car backfiring, a dropped plate, even the distant rumble of thunder – would send a jolt of terror through him, his heart pounding, his body tensing, instantly scanning his surroundings for danger that wasn't there. He started taking circuitous routes to avoid the market square, the very place he once loved, unable to bear the sight of its ongoing reconstruction, the ghosts that lingered there for him.

His work, once his sanctuary and purpose, became a source of profound struggle. He found himself increasingly detached during meetings, his mind drifting back to the image of that child, the helplessness he felt. He’d be talking to a family about their needs, and suddenly the room would blur, replaced by the chaotic scene of the attack. He felt a deep sense of guilt, asking himself repeatedly, "Why me? Why did I survive when so many others didn't?" This guilt was a heavy cloak, smothering his usual optimism and his ability to connect with the people he served. He noticed he was less patient, snapping at colleagues and even his beloved wife, who tried tirelessly to offer comfort. He felt a profound sense of hopelessness, a belief that the world was irrevocably broken and his efforts were futile.

Now, six months on, the symptoms are pervasive. He finds little joy in his once cherished routine. His small garden, once a source of immense pride and peace, has become overgrown; he simply lacks the motivation to tend to it. He isolates himself, spending more time alone, lost in thought. His wife describes him as a different man – quieter, more withdrawn, constantly on edge. He jumps at the slightest sound, his muscles perpetually tense. He struggles to concentrate, whether reading reports for work or trying to follow a conversation with his family. The constant hypervigilance is exhausting, leaving him perpetually fatigued, yet sleep remains elusive. He feels a deep weariness in his bones, a profound sadness that colors every interaction. He wants to be the man he was, the steadfast aid worker, the loving husband, but he feels trapped, unable to escape the lingering shadow of that terrible day.
